## Introduction

The first two pages fit a model whose trees grow but never die. This page
builds a second known-truth study around a monitoring question: **will the
stand hold its adults as the climate changes?** Adults are long-lived, so their
fate is decided by two vital rates that monitoring can measure: how readily
adults recruit new plants, and how many juveniles survive to replace them.

The study fits the present and tests the future:

1. **Survey the present.** Fixed plots, revisited every few years over 20
   years. Every plant on a plot is marked, so each visit finds which marked
   plants survived and which plants are new.
2. **Fit the survey.** SMC-ABC gives the values of the two vital rates
   consistent with it.
3. **Project.** Run the parameter sets the survey supports 40 years forward,
   under each of three climate futures, and test a **management target**: the
   stand keeps at least two-thirds of its adults over the 40 years.

This page builds the study and fits the survey (steps 1 and 2), and projects
the truth to show what the target separates. It also shows why the survey
design matters: a survey that only counts plants, however often it returns,
cannot recover these rates, and marked plots can. The next two pages take step
3: [what it would take](rejection-filter.qmd) to meet the target, with no data,
and the [posterior probability](posterior-property.qmd) of meeting it, given
the survey.

::: {.callout-note}
## Runtime

The first render runs about 800 simulations: the truth's projections, the truth
and 200 prior simulations, 30 more replicates of the truth, and 540 for
SMC-ABC. That is about 4 hours on a laptop, one simulation at a time. Set
`JOSH_BATCH_TARGET` to a batch target profile, such as `gke-test`, and each
batch of simulations is dispatched together to a Kubernetes cluster; there it
took about 2.5 hours, most of it the SMC-ABC search. The runs are stored in the
registry `forevertree_fire.duckdb`, shared by the next two pages, so a later
render replays them without a target.

- **Josh's `batchRemote` takes no seed**, so on a cluster the seeded runs below
  run unseeded. The seed is part of a run's `run_hash`, and the registry, not
  the seed, reproduces it.
- **A search replays exactly only where it ran.** An SMC-ABC search run from
  plain Python proposes different parameter sets from its second generation on
  when replayed under R, which renders these pages: the proposals differ in
  float32's last digits, so their `run_hash`es differ. Run a page's first
  render itself, on the cluster, rather than its searches from a script.

## The Model

The model keeps ForeverTree's landscape: 63 patches of 16 km on a gradient from
wet in the west to dry in the east. Its trees still grow, but they are now born
and die:

- **Adults recruit.** A tree is an adult from 8 years of age. Each year, each
  adult recruits one new tree with chance `recruitment` in a wet year in an
  empty patch, less in drier years and as the patch fills (40 trees at most).
- **Juveniles die more than adults.** An adult dies with chance 2% a year. A
  juvenile dies with chance `juvenileMortality` in a wet year, plus 10% in the
  driest years.
- **Fire.** Fuel grows back in wet years. Each year a patch burns with a chance
  that rises with its fuel, up to 10% at full cover. A fire kills juveniles at
  its intensity (the fuel that burned) and adults at a fifth of it.
- **Patches are on their own.** Seeds don't disperse and fire doesn't spread,
  so a patch that loses its trees stays empty.

Dryness, which recruitment and juvenile deaths read, is linear in a year's rain,
from none at 500 mm to complete at 300 mm. Maturity is by age, not height.

Two parameters are unknown, and the study estimates them (**inverse
parameters**). Everything else is fixed at known values (**direct
parameters**):

| Parameter | Meaning | Prior | Truth |
|-----------|---------|-------|-------|
| `recruitment` | Chance that an adult recruits a tree in a year, at its highest (wet year, empty patch) | Uniform, 10 to 90% | 50% |
| `juvenileMortality` | Chance that a juvenile dies in a wet year | Uniform, 1 to 20% | 5% |

| Fixed | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Age at maturity (`maturityAge`) | 8 years |
| Trees per patch, at most (`maxTrees`) | 40 |
| Adult mortality (`adultMortality`) | 2% a year |
| Added juvenile mortality in the driest years (`droughtMortality`) | 10% |
| Chance of fire at full fuel cover (`fireChance`) | 10% a year |
| Adults a full-intensity fire kills (`adultFireMortality`) | 20% |
| Juveniles a count finds (`juvenileDetection`) | 90% |

# ForeverTree with births, deaths, fuel and fire: the second ForeverTree model.

# age, whatever its height, so the juvenile:adult ratio tracks recruitment and
# survival rather than how fast trees grow. Fuel is a cover % that grows in wet years
# and burns. Each patch is simulated on its own: fire does not spread.
#

  # revisit k years on, the trees aged k + 1 or more were there at the last visit,
  # and those aged k + 8 or more were adults then. Any revisit schedule (k = 1 to

  below2.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 2 years])
  below3.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 3 years])
  below4.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 4 years])
  below5.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 5 years])
  below6.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 6 years])
  below9.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 9 years])
  below10.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 10 years])
  below11.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 11 years])
  below12.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 12 years])
  below13.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 13 years])

  # yearly chance proportional to last year's fuel (fireChance at full cover).
  scheduledFire.step = {
    const sinceFirst = meta.stepCount - meta.firstFire
    const interval = limit meta.fireInterval to [1 count,]  # no division by zero when off
    const onSchedule = floor(sinceFirst / interval) * interval == sinceFirst
    return meta.fireInterval > 0 count and sinceFirst >= 0 count and onSchedule

    (sample uniform from 0% to 100%) < meta.fireChance * prior.fuel / 100%

    prior.fuel + meta.fuelGrowth * (100% - dryness) * (100% - prior.fuel) / 100%

  # and falls as the patch fills. Recruits join at the end of the step.
  openShare.end = limit (1 count - nTrees / meta.maxTrees) to [0 count, 1 count]

    sample binomial
    with n of nAdults
    p of meta.recruitment * (100% - dryness) * openShare / 100%
  ForeverTree.end = prior.ForeverTree | create recruits of ForeverTree

  export.year.step = meta.year
  export.yearsFromSurvey.step = meta.yearsFromSurvey
  export.precipitation.step = precipitation
  export.nAdults.step = nAdults
  export.nJuveniles.step = nJuveniles
  export.below2.step = below2
  export.below3.step = below3
  export.below4.step = below4
  export.below5.step = below5
  export.below6.step = below6
  export.below9.step = below9
  export.below10.step = below10
  export.below11.step = below11
  export.below12.step = below12
  export.below13.step = below13
  export.detectedJuveniles.step =
    sample binomial
    with n of nJuveniles
    p of meta.juvenileDetection
  export.meanHeight.step = mean(ForeverTree.height) if count(ForeverTree) > 0 count else 0 m
  export.fuel.step = fuel
  export.burned.step = burned

  dead.init = false

  clampedTemp.step =
    limit here.temperature
    to [270 K, 330 K]

  temperatureImpact.step =

    from [270 K, 330 K]

  precipImpact.step =
    map here.precipitation
    from [300 mm, 500 mm]
    to [meta.minPrecipImpactPct, 100%] sigmoid

    (sample uniform from 0% to 100%) < deathChance

end organism

# Years of spin-up on resampled historical climate.

# Years of the present: the last historical years, in order. Marked plots are surveyed over
# them, and the final one is the survey year.

# Years of the projection under the future mapped as futureTemperature and futurePrecipitation
# (0: stop at the survey, as fit runs do; at most the future file's 40 years).

# Years in the historical climate files.
historicalYears = 30 count

# --- Growth, as in forevertree.josh ---
# How much can a ForeverTree grow in one year?
maxNewGrowth = 1 m
# How much is growth reduced by drought? (0 %: drought halts growth; 100 %: no effect)
minPrecipImpactPct = 40 %

# --- Demography ---
# Seedlings in each patch at the start of the run.
initialTrees = 10 count
# Most trees a patch holds; recruitment falls to zero as a patch fills.
maxTrees = 40 count
# Age at which a tree is an adult, whatever its height: it recruits, and survives better.
maturityAge = 8 years
# Chance that an adult recruits one tree, in a wet year (500 mm or more) in an empty patch.
recruitment = {{ recruitment }} %
# Chance that an adult dies.
adultMortality = 2 %
# Chance that a juvenile dies, in a wet year.
juvenileMortality = {{ juvenileMortality }} %
# Added to a juvenile's chance of dying in a dry year (300 mm or less); linear in between.
droughtMortality = 10 %

# --- Fuel and fire ---
# Share of the missing fuel cover that grows back in a wet year (less in drier years).
fuelGrowth = 40 %
# Scheduled fire: every fireInterval years from step firstFire, in every patch (0: off).
fireInterval = 0 count
firstFire = 10 count
# Stochastic fire: the yearly chance of fire at full fuel cover, proportional to fuel (0 %: off).
fireChance = 10 %
# Chance that a fire kills an adult, at full fuel cover. Juveniles die at the fuel cover itself.
adultFireMortality = 20 %

# --- Survey ---
# Chance that a survey finds a juvenile (adults are always found).
juvenileDetection = 90 %

````python
"""The fire model's known-truth case study, shared by the Inference pages on replacement.

Put this directory on ``sys.path`` and import it::

    sys.path.insert(0, "examples/sbi_forevertree")
    import forevertree_fire_case as case
    from joshpy.inference import KnownTruthStudy

    registry = RunRegistry("forevertree_fire.duckdb")
    study = KnownTruthStudy(**case.STUDY).load(registry, JoshCLI(josh_jar=JarMode.DEV))

As in ``forevertree_case.py``, joshpy's :class:`~joshpy.inference.KnownTruthStudy`
runs the workflow, and this module holds only what is specific to the model
(forevertree_fire.josh): its prior and truth, the survey, the candidate
statistics, and the projections the hypotheses are about.

Two kinds of run share one model:

- **Fit runs** stop at the survey (``projectionYears = 0``) and need no future
  climate. The truth, the prior simulations and the SMC-ABC search are fit runs.
- **Projections** run 40 more years under one future (``normal``, ``hot_dry`` or
  ``cool_wet``): :func:`projection_model`. Each is a separate run, so its present
  is a fresh realization of its parameters, not a fit run's.

The pseudo-observed data are a **survey of marked plots**: 10 fixed sites,
revisited every ``VISIT_EVERY`` years over the 20-year present. Each visit counts
the adults and juveniles, marks every plant, and finds which of the plants marked
at the last visit survive (by their stage when marked) and which plants are new.
Climate and fires are recorded every year. Adults are always counted; each
juvenile is counted with chance ``juvenileDetection`` (90%), drawn by the model
(``detectedJuveniles``). Marked plants are always refound. The model exports
every present year, so other schedules can be read from the same runs.

Every run writes to ``minio://`` (``exportPrefix`` below), so the same study runs
locally, given MinIO keys in the environment, or on a batch target: set
``JOSH_BATCH_TARGET`` (for example ``gke-test``). Josh's ``batchRemote`` takes no
seed, so on a target the seeds only name the runs, and the registry reproduces
them. After changing this module or the model, re-render the replacement pages
in order (``pixi run docs-inference``).
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import ast
import inspect
import os
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from joshpy.cell_data import DiagnosticQueries
from joshpy.jobs import JobConfig
from joshpy.registry import RunRegistry

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
CLIMATE = HERE / "climate"

TRUTH = {"recruitment": 50.0, "juvenileMortality": 5.0}
PRIOR = {
    "recruitment": {"uniform": [10.0, 90.0]},
    "juvenileMortality": {"uniform": [1.0, 20.0]},
}
TRUTH_SEED = 3  # names the pseudo-observed run (batchRemote takes no seed)
N_PRIOR = 200

# The run (forevertree_fire.jshc.j2): spin-up, present, projection.
SPINUP_YEARS, PRESENT_YEARS, PROJECTION_YEARS = 200, 20, 40
SURVEY_STEP = SPINUP_YEARS + PRESENT_YEARS - 1  # the present's last year
FINAL_STEP = SURVEY_STEP + PROJECTION_YEARS
WINDOW = range(FINAL_STEP - 9, FINAL_STEP + 1)  # the last 10 projected years
FUTURES = ["normal", "hot_dry", "cool_wet"]

# The hypothesis: the adults' yearly growth factor over the projection is at
# least TARGET_LAMBDA, so the stand keeps at least 0.99^40 = 67% of its adults:
# a management target fixed before the analysis. (A fixed juvenile:adult ratio
# target would reward poor juvenile survival: a settled stand's ratio rises as
# its juveniles die faster.)
TARGET_LAMBDA = 0.99

# Fixed survey sites, like monitoring plots: grid positions (x, y) of 10 of the
# 63 patches, two in each of the five western columns, where the trees are.
# x runs west to east (wet to dry), y north to south.
SURVEY_SITES = [
    (0.5, 1.5),
    (0.5, 5.5),
    (1.5, 0.5),
    (1.5, 3.5),
    (2.5, 2.5),
    (2.5, 6.5),
    (3.5, 1.5),
    (3.5, 4.5),
    (4.5, 3.5),
    (4.5, 5.5),
]
DETECTION = 0.9  # juvenileDetection in forevertree_fire.jshc.j2
VISIT_EVERY = 3  # years between visits to the marked plots: steps 201, 204, ..., 219
MAX_TREES, MATURITY_AGE = 40, 8  # maxTrees and maturityAge in forevertree_fire.jshc.j2
# What ABC compares: one statistic per parameter, each built from the model's
# equations, and the stage ratio, which in a settled stand also depends on
# juvenile survival (see statistics() and the fire-model page).
STATISTICS = ["r_hat", "jm_hat", "log_ratio"]


# --- Observation: raw output -> survey -> statistics ---------------------------------


def survey_year(registry: RunRegistry, run_hash: str, replicate: int = 0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Every patch in the survey year: x, y, precipitation, adults, juveniles and detected."""
    cells = DiagnosticQueries(registry).get_all_variables_at_step(SURVEY_STEP, run_hash, replicate)
    if cells.empty:
        raise ValueError(f"No survey-year cells for run {run_hash}, replicate {replicate}")
    cells = cells.rename(
        columns={
            "position_x": "x",
            "position_y": "y",
            "nAdults": "adults",
            "nJuveniles": "juveniles",
            "detectedJuveniles": "detected",
        }
    )
    columns = ["x", "y", "precipitation", "adults", "juveniles", "detected"]
    return cells[columns].sort_values(["y", "x"], ignore_index=True)


def visits(every: int = VISIT_EVERY, years: int = PRESENT_YEARS) -> list[int]:
    """Steps of the visits, every ``every`` years back from the survey year, within ``years``."""
    if not 1 <= every <= 5:
        raise ValueError(f"Revisits every 1 to 5 years are supported, not {every}")
    first = SURVEY_STEP - years + 1
    return sorted(range(SURVEY_STEP, first - 1, -every))


_PRESENTS: dict[tuple[int, str, int], pd.DataFrame] = {}


def present(registry: RunRegistry, run_hash: str, replicate: int = 0) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The surveyed sites in every present year: counts, age structure, rain and fire.

    Read once per run and replicate, so that surveying one run on several
    schedules queries the registry once.
    """
    key = (id(registry), run_hash, replicate)
    if key in _PRESENTS:
        return _PRESENTS[key]
    cells = registry.conn.execute(
        """
        SELECT * FROM cell_data_current
        WHERE run_hash = ? AND replicate = ? AND step BETWEEN ? AND ?
        """,
        [run_hash, replicate, SURVEY_STEP - PRESENT_YEARS + 1, SURVEY_STEP],
    ).df()
    if cells.empty:
        raise ValueError(f"No present years for run {run_hash}, replicate {replicate}")
    cells = cells.rename(
        columns={
            "position_x": "x",
            "position_y": "y",
            "nAdults": "adults",
            "nJuveniles": "juveniles",
            "detectedJuveniles": "detected",
        }
    )
    cells = cells.set_index(["x", "y"]).loc[SURVEY_SITES].reset_index()
    cells["dryness"] = np.clip((500 - cells["precipitation"]) / 200, 0, 1)  # as the model maps it
    cells["burned"] = cells["burned"].astype(str).str.lower().eq("true")
    _PRESENTS[key] = cells = cells.sort_values(["step", "y", "x"], ignore_index=True)
    return cells


def observe(
    registry: RunRegistry,
    run_hash: str,
    replicate: int = 0,
    *,
    detection: bool = True,
    every: int = VISIT_EVERY,
    years: int = PRESENT_YEARS,
) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """The marked-plot survey of one run: one row per site and visit.

    Every visit counts adults and juveniles (``detected``: the juveniles found).
    From the second visit on, a row also records the interval since the last
    visit, k years: the plants marked then (``marked_juveniles``,
    ``marked_adults``), those still alive (``surviving_juveniles``,
    ``surviving_adults``, by their stage when marked), the plants new since
    (``new``), the open space at the last visit (1 - plants / maxTrees), the
    interval's wet years (the sum of 1 - dryness) and whether a fire burned.

    The fates come from the age structure the model exports: a tree is age 1 the
    year it is first counted, so the trees aged k + 1 or more were alive at the
    last visit, and those aged k + maturityAge or more were adults then.

    With ``detection=False``, the survey finds every juvenile (model noise only).
    """
    cells = present(registry, run_hash, replicate)
    steps = visits(every, years)
    at = cells.set_index(["step", "x", "y"])
    rows = []
    for i, step in enumerate(steps):
        now = at.loc[step]
        row = pd.DataFrame(
            {
                "step": step,
                "adults": now["adults"],
                "juveniles": now["juveniles"],
                "detected": now["detected"] if detection else now["juveniles"],
            }
        )
        if i > 0:
            last, k = at.loc[steps[i - 1]], step - steps[i - 1]
            between = cells[cells["step"].between(steps[i - 1], step - 1)].groupby(["x", "y"])
            plants = now["adults"] + now["juveniles"]
            row["marked_juveniles"] = last["juveniles"]
            row["marked_adults"] = last["adults"]
            row["surviving_juveniles"] = now[f"below{k + MATURITY_AGE}"] - now[f"below{k + 1}"]
            row["surviving_adults"] = plants - now[f"below{k + MATURITY_AGE}"]
            row["new"] = now[f"below{k + 1}"]
            row["open_space"] = (1 - (last["adults"] + last["juveniles"]) / MAX_TREES).clip(lower=0)
            row["wet_years"] = k - between["dryness"].sum()  # the sum of 1 - dryness
            row["burned"] = between["burned"].any()
        rows.append(row.reset_index())
    return pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)


def statistics(survey: pd.DataFrame) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Candidate summary statistics of a marked-plot survey.

    From the fates of marked plants, one statistic per parameter, each following
    the model's equations:

    - ``r_hat``: new plants per marked adult, per wet year, per unit of open
      space, in %. Recruits ~ Binomial(adults, recruitment x (1 - dryness) x open
      space), so this tracks ``recruitment`` (below it: recruits that die before
      the next visit are never seen).
    - ``jm_hat``: the yearly death rate of marked juveniles, over intervals
      without fire, in %. A juvenile dies with chance juvenileMortality + dryness x
      droughtMortality, so this tracks ``juvenileMortality``.

    From the counts alone, as a survey without marked plants would have, each
    pooled over the visits: ``log_ratio`` (juveniles found per adult),
    ``adult_density`` (adults per site) and ``density_gradient`` (log adults at
    the four dry sites minus the four wet ones). Pooled counts get half a plant,
    so that an empty survey still has a finite log, and the rates get a
    pseudo-observation.
    """
    intervals = survey.dropna(subset=["new"]) if "new" in survey else survey.iloc[:0]
    wet, dry = survey[survey["x"] < 2], survey[survey["x"] > 3]
    out = {
        "log_ratio": float(
            np.log((survey["detected"].sum() + 0.5) / (survey["adults"].sum() + 0.5))
        ),
        "adult_density": float(survey["adults"].mean()),
        "density_gradient": float(
            np.log(dry["adults"].sum() + 0.5) - np.log(wet["adults"].sum() + 0.5)
        ),
        "r_hat": np.nan,
        "jm_hat": np.nan,
    }
    if not intervals.empty:
        k = int(np.diff(np.unique(survey["step"]))[0])
        exposure = intervals["marked_adults"] * intervals["open_space"] * intervals["wet_years"]
        unburned = intervals[~intervals["burned"].astype(bool)]
        survival = (unburned["surviving_juveniles"].sum() + 0.9**k) / (
            unburned["marked_juveniles"].sum() + 1
        )
        out["r_hat"] = float(100 * (intervals["new"].sum() + 0.5) / (exposure.sum() + 1))
        out["jm_hat"] = float(100 * (1 - min(survival, 1.0) ** (1 / k)))
    return out

def landscape(registry: RunRegistry, run_hashes: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Juveniles and adults over the whole landscape, by run, replicate and step.

    Columns run_hash, replicate, step, years (since the survey), adults,
    juveniles and ratio (juveniles per adult; NaN without adults).
    """
    totals = registry.conn.execute(
        """
        SELECT run_hash, replicate, step,
               SUM(nAdults) AS adults, SUM(nJuveniles) AS juveniles
        FROM cell_data_current
        WHERE run_hash IN (SELECT unnest(?))
        GROUP BY ALL
        ORDER BY run_hash, replicate, step
        """,
        [list(run_hashes)],
    ).df()
    totals["years"] = totals["step"] - SURVEY_STEP
    totals["ratio"] = totals["juveniles"] / totals["adults"].where(totals["adults"] > 0)
    return totals


_LANDSCAPES: dict[tuple[int, str], pd.DataFrame] = {}


def _run_landscape(registry: RunRegistry, run_hash: str, replicate: int) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """One run's landscape, read once for all its replicates (a filter measures each)."""
    key = (id(registry), run_hash)
    years = _LANDSCAPES.get(key)
    if years is None or replicate not in set(years["replicate"]):  # new, or topped up since
        years = _LANDSCAPES[key] = landscape(registry, [run_hash])
    return years


def projected(registry: RunRegistry, run_hash: str, replicate: int) -> dict[str, float]:
    """One projection's measurements: the ratio over the window, and the adults' growth rate.

    - ``ratio``: the landscape's juveniles per adult, averaged over the last 10
      projected years (NaN if the adults died out);
    - ``adult_lambda``: the adults' yearly growth factor from the survey to the
      last projected year, (A_final / A_survey)^(1/40).

    if FINAL_STEP not in years.index:
        raise ValueError(f"Run {run_hash}, replicate {replicate} is not a projection")
    adults = years["adults"]
    return {
        "ratio": float(years.loc[list(WINDOW), "ratio"].mean(skipna=False)),
        "adult_lambda": float(
            (adults[FINAL_STEP] / adults[SURVEY_STEP]) ** (1 / PROJECTION_YEARS)
            if adults[SURVEY_STEP] > 0
            else np.nan
        ),
    }

## The Climate and Its Futures

The climate is synthetic, made for this study: yearly rain and mean
temperature on a grid over the landscape (generated outside joshpy; each NetCDF
file in `examples/sbi_forevertree/climate/` records its seed).
`preprocess_climate.py` writes them onto the model's patches. Rain falls from
about 550 mm in the west to 230 mm in the east, and wet and dry years are
mostly shared across the landscape, so recruitment comes in pulses.

Each run has three parts:

| Part | Years | Climate |
|------|-------|---------|
| Spin-up | 200 | Historical years drawn at random from 30 |
| Present | 20 | The last 20 historical years, in order; the survey's years |
| Projection | 40 | One future: `normal`, `hot_dry` or `cool_wet` |

The futures start the year after the survey:

- **`normal`** continues the historical climate.
- **`hot_dry`** ramps to about 26% less rain and 1.8 K warmer by its last
  decade.
- **`cool_wet`** ramps to about 16% more rain and 0.9 K cooler.

Fit runs stop at the end of the present (`projectionYears = 0`) and read no
future. A projection is a separate run, `case.projection_model(future)`: the
same model run 40 years further, with that future's files mapped. Temperature
changes only growth, and growth doesn't set maturity, so here a future acts on
the stand through its rain.

near the truth meet it, and sets with fewer recruits or more juvenile deaths do
not. Whether the survey can tell them apart is what the rest of this page, and

## The Pseudo-Observed Data: Marked Plots

A monitoring program returns to fixed plots, and on a marked plot it tags every
plant, so that at the next visit it can tell the survivors from the newcomers.
The pseudo-observed data are such a **survey**:

- **10 fixed sites**, two in each of the five western columns, where the trees
  are (from about 550 mm of rain to 400 mm);
- **visited every 3 years over the 20-year present**, seven visits in all
  (`case.visits()`);
- at each visit, the **adults and the juveniles found**: adults always, each
  juvenile with chance 90%;
- from the second visit on, the **fates of the plants marked at the last
  visit**: which survive, by their stage when marked, and which plants are new.
  Marked plants are always refound.
- the **rain and fires of every year**, which a program records anyway.

The model draws the counts' detection itself, as in the
[first case study](forevertree.qmd#the-pseudo-observed-data-a-survey): the
observer is simulated with the system [@zurell2010], so the same survey applies
to the truth and to every simulation.

```josh
export.detectedJuveniles.step =
  sample binomial
  with n of nJuveniles
  p of meta.juvenileDetection
```

Josh exports patches, not individual trees. A marked plot can still be read
from the patches' **age structure**: the model exports how many live trees are
younger than each of a few ages, and a tree is 1 year old the first year it is
counted. So at a revisit k years on, the trees aged k + 1 or more were there at
the last visit, those aged k + 8 or more were adults then, and the rest are
new:

```josh
below4.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 4 years])
below11.start = count(ForeverTree[ForeverTree.age < 11 years])
```

Every present year is exported, so any schedule of revisits every 1 to 5 years
can be read from the same runs: [What a Survey Can Know](#what-a-survey-can-know)
compares them.

````python

        raise ValueError(f"Revisits every 1 to 5 years are supported, not {every}")

    """

    at = cells.set_index(["step", "x", "y"])

## Choosing Summary Statistics

The [first case study's process](forevertree.qmd#choosing-among-them) asks for
statistics that move with the parameters, roughly one per parameter, and
finally a test of sufficiency on simulated data. On the first model, the CV of
the heights divided growth out and tracked drought sensitivity: a statistic
read off the model's equation. Here too the best statistics come from the
model's equations, turned around:

- **Recruits.** Each year an adult recruits with chance
  `recruitment` × (1 − dryness) × (1 − plants / 40). So new plants per marked
  adult, per wet year, per unit of open space, track `recruitment`. They track
  it from below, since recruits that die before the next visit are never seen,
  but they are computed the same way for every simulation, which is all ABC
  needs.
- **Juvenile deaths.** A juvenile dies with chance `juvenileMortality` +
  10% × dryness, or in a fire. So the yearly death rate of marked juveniles,
  over intervals without fire, tracks `juvenileMortality`.

Beside them, three statistics a survey without marked plants would have:

| Statistic | Definition | Describes |
|-----------|------------|-----------|
| `r_hat` | New plants per (marked adult × wet year × open space), %, over all intervals | Recruitment per adult |
| `jm_hat` | Yearly death rate of marked juveniles over intervals without fire, % | Juvenile survival |
| `log_ratio` | $\log\big((J + \tfrac12) / (A + \tfrac12)\big)$, juveniles found $J$ and adults $A$, over all sites and visits | The stage ratio |
| `adult_density` | Adults per site, over all visits | How full the stand is |
| `density_gradient` | $\log(A + \tfrac12)$ at the 4 dry sites minus at the 4 wet sites, over all visits | How far east the stand reaches |

````python
def statistics(survey: pd.DataFrame) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Candidate summary statistics of a marked-plot survey.

    From the fates of marked plants, one statistic per parameter, each following
    the model's equations:

    - ``r_hat``: new plants per marked adult, per wet year, per unit of open
      space, in %. Recruits ~ Binomial(adults, recruitment x (1 - dryness) x open
      space), so this tracks ``recruitment`` (below it: recruits that die before
      the next visit are never seen).
    - ``jm_hat``: the yearly death rate of marked juveniles, over intervals
      without fire, in %. A juvenile dies with chance juvenileMortality + dryness x
      droughtMortality, so this tracks ``juvenileMortality``.

    From the counts alone, as a survey without marked plants would have, each
    pooled over the visits: ``log_ratio`` (juveniles found per adult),
    ``adult_density`` (adults per site) and ``density_gradient`` (log adults at
    the four dry sites minus the four wet ones). Pooled counts get half a plant,
    so that an empty survey still has a finite log, and the rates get a
    pseudo-observation.
    """
    intervals = survey.dropna(subset=["new"]) if "new" in survey else survey.iloc[:0]
    wet, dry = survey[survey["x"] < 2], survey[survey["x"] > 3]
    out = {
        "log_ratio": float(
            np.log((survey["detected"].sum() + 0.5) / (survey["adults"].sum() + 0.5))
        ),
        "adult_density": float(survey["adults"].mean()),
        "density_gradient": float(
            np.log(dry["adults"].sum() + 0.5) - np.log(wet["adults"].sum() + 0.5)
        ),
        "r_hat": np.nan,
        "jm_hat": np.nan,
    }
    if not intervals.empty:
        k = int(np.diff(np.unique(survey["step"]))[0])
        exposure = intervals["marked_adults"] * intervals["open_space"] * intervals["wet_years"]
        unburned = intervals[~intervals["burned"].astype(bool)]
        survival = (unburned["surviving_juveniles"].sum() + 0.9**k) / (
            unburned["marked_juveniles"].sum() + 1
        )
        out["r_hat"] = float(100 * (intervals["new"].sum() + 0.5) / (exposure.sum() + 1))
        out["jm_hat"] = float(100 * (1 - min(survival, 1.0) ** (1 / k)))
    return out
````

### Testing sufficiency on simulated data

The leave-one-out check of the [SMC-ABC page](smc-abc.qmd#calibration-a-coverage-check)
says how much a set of statistics tells about each parameter, from the
reference table alone: each prior simulation in turn plays the observed data,
and the 20 closest of the others are accepted. A width near 1 means the
statistics say nothing about the parameter.

The check has a floor. With 200 simulations, the 20 closest span part of the
prior even when the statistics determine the parameters exactly. Scoring the
parameters themselves as statistics shows where it lies:


::: {.cell}

```{.python .cell-code}
def width_floor(k=20):
    """Leave-one-out widths if the statistics were the parameters themselves."""
    theta = study.reference[list(case.PRIOR)].to_numpy()
    z = (theta - theta.mean(axis=0)) / theta.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
    level = (k - 1) / (k + 1)
    spans = np.array([level * (spec["uniform"][1] - spec["uniform"][0]) for spec in case.PRIOR.values()])
    widths = []
    for i in range(len(z)):
        distance = np.sqrt(((z - z[i]) ** 2).sum(axis=1))
        distance[i] = np.inf
        accepted = theta[np.argsort(distance, kind="stable")[:k]]
        widths.append((accepted.max(axis=0) - accepted.min(axis=0)) / spans)
    return pd.Series(np.mean(widths, axis=0), index=list(case.PRIOR), name="width")


width_floor().round(3)
```

## Fitting the Present: SMC-ABC

The fit is the [SMC-ABC page](smc-abc.qmd)'s, on the three statistics: 60
initial draws, 30 particles and 600 simulations. On a batch target, each round
of proposals is one batch, and SMC-ABC's `"measured"` batch policy sizes the
rounds from the acceptance rate it has measured, so that each generation takes
about two rounds instead of one per missing particle. The policy changes which
parameter sets are proposed, so the search names it, and a replay without a
target proposes the same runs:


::: {.cell}

print(f"{len(evaluated)} evaluations, {result.failed} failed; {len(reused)} reused prior simulations")

The posterior contains the truth and centres near it: `recruitment` 53% (90%
interval 41 to 67%) and `juvenileMortality` 6.2% (2.4 to 11.2%). It narrows
`recruitment` to about a third of the prior and `juvenileMortality` to about
half. Most particles sit close to the cross. The heaviest, at about 67% and
11%, is a parameter set with more recruits and more juvenile deaths than the
truth. Its weight is large because few proposals landed near it, and it
stretches the upper end of both intervals. The effective sample size, 22.9 of
30, says the weights are even enough for these summaries to be stable.

This is what the second model was built to show: with statistics read off the
model's equations, and a survey that records births and deaths, the fit recovers
the truth. It is calibrated, but not narrow. The survey's 10 sites leave about a
third of the prior for `recruitment` and half for `juvenileMortality`. The next
page asks what the target needs, and the last whether this posterior is narrow
enough to answer it.
